title: {{NAME}} and the Princess Who Needed an Engineer
moral: The greatest problem-solvers are the ones who ask good questions.

pages.content:
The message arrived by royal carrier pigeon, which was unusual, and was marked URGENT in red wax, which was more unusual, and smelled faintly of motor oil, which was extremely unusual for a royal document.

Hi. My name is Princess Theodora. My royal clockwork orchestra has stopped working. The royal ball is in three days. My mechanical advisor has quit. Please help. — T

{{NAME}} had never been to a palace before. He packed his toolkit and took the bus.

pages.content:
The clockwork orchestra was extraordinary: twelve mechanical musicians, each one intricate and exact, capable of playing any piece with perfect timing.

They had all stopped at precisely the same moment, mid-bar, in the middle of a waltz.

{{NAME}} examined the nearest one carefully, then looked at all twelve, then walked the room thinking.

"What happened just before they stopped?" he asked Princess Theodora.

"The lights went out briefly," she said. "Just a flicker."

"Power surge," said {{NAME}}. "They all share a timing circuit. One glitch froze them all."

pages.content:
The timing circuit was deep in the floor beneath the orchestra, accessible through a panel behind the conductor's podium.

{{NAME}} and Princess Theodora worked side by side: she held the torch and passed tools because she had read every manual the previous engineer had left, and he worked the circuit because he had small steady hands and could see what needed doing.

They were a good team. She anticipated what he would need two steps ahead. He told her why each step mattered.

By hour three, the timing crystal was reset.

pages.content:
The moment the circuit came back online, all twelve musicians began exactly where they had stopped: the middle bar of the waltz, as if three days had not passed.

Princess Theodora burst out laughing. Then she stood up very straight, composed herself, and said: "That is the finest engineering I have witnessed."

"It was the finest torchholding," said {{NAME}}. "I couldn't have found the crystal without you."

She smiled at him. "You should stay and teach my next engineer."

"Three days?" he said.

"Three weeks," she said firmly.

pages.content:
He stayed three weeks.

The princess turned out to be the best student he'd ever taught: she asked questions nobody else would have thought to ask, and remembered every answer perfectly.

On the last night before he went home, the orchestra played just for the two of them, a waltz that filled the empty ballroom.

{{NAME}} lay in the palace guest room that night with his toolkit by the bed, listening to the distant music still drifting through the halls.

He was nearly asleep when he heard one last, perfect note: the orchestra finishing its piece, right on time.
